newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hague judges complete visit to disputed Danube dam.
newsitem.headline: Hague judges complete visit to disputed Danube dam.

text.p: Judges from the International Court of Justice on Friday completed a four-day visit to Slovakia and Hungary as part of efforts to appraise the effects of Slovakia's controversial $1 billion Danube dam project.

The visit, marking the first time the court has left its base in the Hague, is part of proceedings under way to decide whether Slovakia was right to proceed with the Gabcikovo project and whether Hungary was entitled to pull out of an earlier joint plan.
"Coming here was a very good idea," one of the judges, Karl Fleischauer, told Reuters after being welcomed in Hungary's parliament by Prime Minister Gyula Horn.

"The visit must be judged a success," the court's president, Stephen Schwebel said. "A picture is worth a thousand words and we have seen many sights, and at the same there has been no lack of words."
The long-running dispute over the Gabcikovo project has strained relations between Budapest and Bratislava.
The dam was originally part of a 1977 plan agreed by the then Communist governments of Czechoslovakia and Hungary to harness the Danube waters, which forms the border between Hungary and Slovakia.
But Hungary suspended work on a companion dam downstream at Nagymaros in 1989 after pressure from environmental groups. In 1992 it pulled out of the project altogether.
Slovakia pressed ahead with the hydroelectric scheme at Gabcikovo after its split from Czechoslovakia in 1993 but it agreed to submit the dispute to the U.N. court.

It says Hungary broke its part of the agreement and should pay damages to Slovakia, arguing that Budapest made the environmental problems worse by halting construction of the Nagymaros dam which would have offset the effects of Gabcikovo.
Hungary told the Court the project was wreaking havoc on the environment and depriving Hungarians of vital water resources.

This week the 15 judges inspected the Gabcikovo hydroelectric power plant, which produces up to 12 percent of Slovakia's energy needs, the flood plain of Szigetkoz, which Hungary says has suffered badly from a lowering of the water table, and the reclaimed Nagymaros site.

The two sides presented their initial cases in March and will have a second chance to address the court later this month, with Hungary winding up its case on April 11 and Slovakia concluding proceedings on April 15.
The Court is not expected to deliver its verdict before September.
